title: Executive legal interpretation when judicial review is unavailable
shortTitle: Executive legal interpretation when judicial review is unavailable
summary: Government lawyers often provide the only practical legal review of executive decisions and therefore have a distinct advisory responsibility.
notes:
Executive officials may have the final practical word because a decision is legally unreviewable, too obscure to attract challenge, or insufficiently connected to an identifiable injured plaintiff. The reading gives nonenforcement decisions and allocation within lump-sum appropriations as examples connected to Heckler v. Chaney and Lincoln v. Vigil. It also distinguishes exclusive constitutional choices from statutory decisions placed beyond review. Those categories explain why absence of a judicial remedy does not establish unlimited substantive authority.

Peter Shane argues that government lawyers serving as advisers should interpret law conscientiously and with a degree of objective judgment because no court or oversight body may ever review the result. He distinguishes that advisory role from advocacy in litigation before an independent judge. The Office of Legal Counsel’s role in settling executive-branch legal disputes makes the institutional issue especially important. This is the author’s normative argument, supported by the practical structure of review, and is not presented as a separate judicial holding.
